title: Flashcards: finite study sessions
focus: session snapshots, state transitions and persistence failure
model: Cards have stable ids, deck, front, back and known. A session holds a snapshot of eligible ids, a cursor and a revealed-answer flag. Saved cards and temporary session state serve different purposes.
before: Grading the last card never advanced beyond it. Changing decks during study retained the old order, and there was no unlearned-only study option.
after: Study can select unlearned cards only, changing decks restarts the session, and the final grade produces an explicit completion state. Grading requires revealing the answer. Failed storage leaves the card and cursor unchanged.
example: JS contains a unknown and b known; CSS contains c unknown. Select JS and unlearned-only: the session contains just a. Reveal and mark it known: progress becomes Completed 1 of 1 and grading is disabled. Restarting now finds no eligible cards. A rejected write instead keeps a at index zero.
concept: A session should not continuously recompute its order from changing known flags. If grading immediately removed a card from a live filtered array, incrementing the cursor could skip the next card. Snapshot ids at session start, then look up each card by identity. The cursor may equal the length: that represents completion, not a value to hide by clamping it to the last index. Reveal-before-grade is another state transition. The disabled button communicates the rule, while the handler guard protects repeated or direct invocation. Write the changed known flag before advancing. Only knowledge flags persist; the current session does not resume after reload. A missed card is revisited in a new session, not repeatedly inserted into this one. Those are product choices to explain before adding spaced repetition.
flow: Storage succeeds before publishing or advancing
The renderer distinguishes empty, active and complete
exercises: Add a restart button preserving original order.
Test a failed grade followed by a successful retry.
Design spaced repetition and saved-data migration.
answers: Call startStudy(false), retain the deck/filter and test completion followed by restart.
Store this session's grades keyed by id; do not infer them from flags saved in earlier sessions.
Reject setItem once, restore the writer, retry and verify one cursor increment and one saved result.
Choose a scheduling rule, store due dates separately from order and migrate old known-only records deliberately.
setup: Open index.html in a browser. From this project folder run `npm install`, then `npm test` with Node 22 or a compatible later version for the DOM tests.

title: Habit Tracker: calendar streaks
focus: local dates, derived statistics and edge cases
model: Each habit has a history map from YYYY-MM-DD to true. Current and best streaks are derived values, not independently persisted counters.
before: The current streak required today to be checked already, and there was no longest historical streak.
after: A current streak may continue through yesterday while today is still in progress. The best badge counts consecutive real dates, ignoring invalid, false and future entries. Day buttons have full accessible names.
example: Checks on February 28, February 29 and March 1, 2024 give best three. Add March 3 and invalid February 30: best remains three. With today March 11, checks on March 9 and 10 give current two; a check only on March 9 gives zero.
concept: Neighboring local midnights may be 23 or 25 hours apart at daylight-saving changes. The history stores calendar labels, so bestStreak maps validated labels to UTC day ordinals only to compare adjacency. It does not reinterpret the habit as a UTC activity. Reject impossible dates by round-tripping their calendar representation: JavaScript may normalize February 30 into March. Sort ordinals, increase a run for a difference of one, reset it at a gap, and retain the maximum. Current streak uses local today and permits yesterday as an anchor because the user still has today to complete the habit. A complete missed day breaks it. Explain this rule rather than presenting it as the only possible definition of streak.
flow: Sort day ordinals and scan runs
Calculate current from today or yesterday
exercises: Show the best streak start and end dates.
Extend the visible grid to 30 days.
Refresh an open page across midnight.
answers: Track runStart and the winning range, choosing and testing a tie policy.
Parameterize the window and its denominator; keep best streak based on all history.
Use consecutive date labels around the fall transition and expect adjacency despite 25 elapsed hours.
Compute the next local midnight with calendar setters, refresh and reschedule; do not assume a fixed 24-hour delay.

title: Reading List: composed views
focus: filter composition, deterministic ordering and summaries
model: Saved books contain id, title, author, status, rating and notes. Search, status filter and sorting are temporary view state.
before: Search and sorting existed without an explicit status filter or matching-versus-overall summary. Equal ratings relied on source order.
after: Status filtering composes with search and sorting. Rating ties use title then id. The live summary distinguishes visible books from overall finished count, and sorting preserves saved order.
example: Zebra and Alpha both have rating five and Finished status; Beta is Reading. Filter Finished, search Maya and sort by rating: Alpha then Zebra appear. Saved order remains Zebra, Alpha, Beta. An unmatched query shows zero results while overall finished stays two.
concept: A view is a projection of authoritative data. Combine predicates with AND so matching search text cannot bypass the selected status. Compute the matching count from the projection and the finished count from all books. JavaScript sort mutates its input; the spread copy protects the saved array. Deterministic ties keep the display understandable when scores match. Comparing titles after ratings expresses a user-facing order, while id is a final stable tie-breaker. Tests inspect headings and serialized order because either alone misses part of the guarantee. Filters reset on reload; this change does not persist preferences or merge duplicate books.
flow: Copy and filter the book collection
Compute visible and overall counts separately
Show the empty state when appropriate
exercises: Test an edit that leaves the selected status.
Introduce a deliberate locale sorting policy.
answers: Derive author choices from all books and add another AND predicate; test mismatched author versus matching text.
Version and validate the preferences without rewriting book records.
Change a Finished book to Reading; it should leave the view but remain saved with the same id.
Use Intl.Collator with stated locale/options and fixtures containing accents and digit sequences.

title: Note Vault: durable serialized writes
focus: async queues, atomic file replacement and repositories
model: A JSON file owns the note array. One repository instance owns a promise tail ordering every read-modify-write. Identity survives edits and restarts.
before: Concurrent operations could read the same file version and overwrite each other. Direct target writes risked truncation. The client imported a component without mounting React.
after: Operations serialize through one queue. Writes use a unique sibling file and rename after writing succeeds. Failure preserves old bytes and does not poison later operations. HTTP errors are handled and Vite mounts the client correctly.
example: With one welcome note, twelve concurrent creates leave thirteen records. Pin four created ids: those four are pinned independently of the welcome note. Reject a rename, compare original bytes, retry successfully and reopen the repository to read the result.
concept: Serializing only writeFile is too late if two callers already read the same old array. A queue item must encompass read, mutation and write. Chaining onto tail establishes order. Assigning tail to result.catch keeps the queue usable while returning the original result lets the caller observe rejection. An exclusive unique sibling temporary file is written before rename changes the visible target. This does not provide a transaction across files, power-loss durability or cross-process locking. One app owns one repository; multiple workers need shared coordination or a database. Malformed JSON is an error to investigate, not a reason to reseed and overwrite data. Only ENOENT triggers initial seeding. The concurrency fixture must count the created ids, since the seeded welcome note is also pinned and its body contains the word note.
flow: Write a sibling file and rename
Return success or a handled error while keeping the queue usable
answers: Two serial toggles restore the initial flag; verify the complete record and identity.
Reject writeFile once and verify unchanged target bytes and cleanup of the owned temporary file.
Read through the queue instead of independently inspecting a file during replacement.
Preserve the repository contract, migrate notes once and run the same contract tests against both adapters.
setup: From the project root run `npm install`, `npm run dev`, `npm test`, and `npm run build` as needed. Vite serves client/ and the API defaults to port 4106. Normal startup creates server/data/notes.json if absent; tests use disposable temporary files. Run one port-4106 project at a time.

title: Budget Tracker: cents and safe commits
focus: numeric parsing, representations and persisted state
model: Stored amounts retain the original dollar-number format. New input is parsed into bounded cents, and totals accumulate rounded cents before dollar formatting.
before: Number conversion and <= 0 did not reject all malformed values. Direct decimal accumulation complicated totals, and failed writes could put memory ahead of storage.
after: New amounts require positive bounded decimal text with at most two fractional digits and real dates. Totals accumulate cents. Create, edit and delete publish only after storage succeeds, retaining the form on failure.
example: Income 0.10 plus 0.20 displays $0.30; 1.01 parses to 101 cents. Reject empty, zero, negative, 1.001, Infinity, scientific notation and values above 999999999.99. A failed edit to 12.50 keeps the prior amount and the entered form value.
concept: Number inputs supply text. Define its grammar before conversion: Number accepts forms that do not belong in this currency workflow. Split whole and fractional text, right-pad the fraction and construct integer minor units. Do not multiply arbitrary fractional input and assume an exact result. Existing saved dollars remain compatible; each total contribution is rounded to cents first. This is not a versioned migration or arbitrary-precision ledger. Extremely large collections can exceed safe aggregate limits, and legacy malformed storage is not automatically repaired. Committing state is a separate boundary: serialize the full candidate, write it, then publish it. Stable ids distinguish an edit from accidental insertion.
answers: Explain precision, range and required-value failures beside the associated input with an accepted example.
Group the same cent representation and keep overall totals independent of view filters.
Reject setItem and assert the record remains visible and persisted with useful feedback.
Choose rounding explicitly, preserve unconvertible raw data for review and prove migration happens once.

title: Pantry Inventory: expiration versus stock
focus: independent predicates, calendar rules and validation
model: Quantity, minimum and expiration are separate fields. Low means quantity <= minimum. Expired means the YYYY-MM-DD label is earlier than local today.
before: Fresh really meant above the stock threshold, so an expired item could appear fresh. Some invalid numeric values passed validation.
after: Rows show stock and expiration independently. Expired filtering is available, and the in-stock/nonexpired view excludes expired items. New quantities must be finite and nonnegative, dates must be real, and returning to the tab refreshes date-based status.
example: On September 8, an item expiring September 7 with quantity five and minimum one is Stock OK and Expired. An item expiring today with quantity one and minimum one is Low stock and not expired. Only a future sufficiently stocked item matches the combined view.
concept: A single status can hide independent dimensions. Compute low and expired separately and compose them for each view. Equality at the stock threshold is intentional: stock equal to minimum is already low. Equality at the date boundary has a different rule: this app treats the labeled date as valid through that day. Valid ISO labels sort chronologically, so string comparison is useful only after date validation. Reading local year, month and day avoids a UTC conversion that could shift the calendar label. This is an inventory software rule, not food-safety guidance. Visibility refresh does not schedule an exact update at midnight in a continuously visible tab. Existing malformed storage is not automatically migrated.
flow: Refresh derived status when the tab returns
exercises: Add an expired count beside low stock.
answers: Choose inclusive boundaries and build them with calendar addition; test today and the seventh day.
Count each predicate independently; an item may contribute to both.
Use fixed local dates around February 29 and avoid toISOString when deriving expected local labels.
Compute next local midnight with calendar setters, clear/reschedule the timer and avoid a fixed 24-hour assumption.

title: Snippet Vault: storage and clipboard failure
focus: ES modules, normalization and rejected promises
model: The store owns snippets, main.js owns forms and views, and dom.js owns rendering/clipboard work. Tags retain their first display spelling while deduplicating lowercase comparison keys.
before: The store mutated before writing, duplicate tag variants accumulated, and rejected clipboard promises could escape without feedback.
after: Create, edit and delete publish only after persistence succeeds. Tags deduplicate case-insensitively, missing edit ids and blank content are rejected, and clipboard denial returns false so the UI can explain failure.
example: Tags Utility,utility, EVENTS,events become Utility and EVENTS. A failed title-edit write leaves saved and in-memory titles unchanged. Clipboard rejection resolves false instead of producing an unhandled rejection.
concept: A useful module boundary owns a coherent responsibility. The store decides when data changes; rendering should not guess whether storage succeeded. Construct the candidate, write it and only then assign the module variable. If serialization or storage throws, assignment is skipped and the UI preserves the form. A Set of comparison keys removes duplicate tags while the first original spelling remains visible. Feature detection for navigator.clipboard is not permission: writeText may still reject, so the helper handles the asynchronous failure. Tests import actual ES modules under a fresh module identity for each fixture. Read methods still return object references; this change does not claim deep immutability against callers mutating those objects themselves.
flow: Reject blank content or missing edit ids
exercises: Test clipboard absence and denial separately.
answers: Copy records and tag arrays and test attempted mutation through a returned value.
Compare normalized tags while keeping display spelling; compose with existing filters.
Provide one fixture without the API and one whose promise rejects; neither should claim a successful copy.
Validate the entire envelope and all records before one commit, keeping ids and old state on failure.
setup: Serve the project over HTTP with `python -m http.server 8000`, then open http://localhost:8000. ES modules cannot be opened through file://. Run `npm test` with Node 22 for the module checks.

title: Room Booking: editable reservations and time boundaries
focus: half-open intervals, database constraints and timezones
model: Bookings link a room UUID to a title, bookedBy label and two instants. PostgreSQL stores timestamptz and enforces room-specific nonoverlap using a GiST exclusion constraint.
before: The UI could not edit although PUT existed. Runtime checks accepted malformed types or ambiguous timestamps, and local slot defaults mishandled midnight rollover.
after: The UI edits existing ids and converts local input to explicit instants. The API validates ids, bounded text, real timestamps and forward windows. Day views send browser-local boundaries; a legacy date query explicitly means a UTC day. Database overlap enforcement is verified under concurrency and failed edits.
example: Two requests for one room from 10:00 to 11:00 UTC yield one 201 and one 409. An adjacent 11:00-to-12:00 slot succeeds. Extending the first to 11:30 fails and preserves its old end. Renaming preserves its id. A query window ending at 11:00 excludes the adjacent slot.
concept: Half-open intervals include their start and exclude their end, so adjacent meetings can share a boundary. A check-then-insert in application code has a race; the database constraint is the final arbiter. A failed UPDATE preserves the previous row. datetime-local has no timezone, so the browser converts it to an ISO instant before submission. A local day is represented by two independently computed midnights, which can be 23 or 25 hours apart. The explicit legacy UTC-day policy avoids depending on a database session timezone. bookedBy is a human label, not authentication: this demo does not enforce ownership. Runtime validation gives helpful errors, while the constraint protects integrity even for competing writes. An overlap test and a failed-update test prove different postconditions.
flow: Load an existing booking into the editor
Convert local inputs to ISO instants
Validate UUIDs, text and time range
Refresh the schedule after an identity-preserving update
answers: Condition the update on an expected version; the overlap constraint cannot detect lost edits.
Include dates when local start/end days differ, with accessible full timestamps.
Construct local midnight and next midnight in a fixed timezone and assert the UTC instants sent.
Use a verified caller identity and stored owner id at each access boundary, keeping bookedBy as separate display text.
setup: Install dependencies at the project root. Configure DATABASE_URL for a new empty development database. The existing db:setup script resets its tables, so use it only for that disposable setup. Run `npm run dev`, `npm run build` and `npm run typecheck` at the root. Tests use a separate astra_test_* database and run with `npm test` at the root.

## Database test setup

Create a dedicated PostgreSQL database such as astra_test_learning. Set your own test credentials in PowerShell:

```powershell
$env:ASTRA_TEST_DATABASE_URL = 'postgres://YOUR_TEST_USER:YOUR_TEST_PASSWORD@127.0.0.1:5432/astra_test_learning'
```

Tests reject differently named databases. The user must be allowed to create schemas. Each run creates and drops only its unique schema. Room Booking additionally enables btree_gist and pgcrypto in this dedicated test database; it does not run the scaffold's DROP TABLE statements against a fallback namespace. Run npm test from the Room Booking root or the Notes/Bookmark server folder. Interrupted runs can leave owned schemas; inspect the dedicated database before cleaning them up. Configuration must precede importing the app's database module.

title: Notes API: actual content search
focus: PostgreSQL text search, runtime validation and stale responses
model: Notes have title, body, folder, status and JSON tags. Search indexes the meaning of title/body; folder/status are independent exact filters, and internal ids/timestamps do not participate.
before: The API cast a whole row to text, and the UI searched serialized JSON locally. Internal metadata could match a document query. Payload field types were not enforced.
after: English to_tsvector/plainto_tsquery search uses bound parameters over title/body. The UI debounces requests and ignores older responses. Payloads and filters are bounded, tags serialize correctly to JSON, and partial edits retain omitted fields.
example: Running notes matches search run through stemming. A note whose folder is HiddenKeyword does not match that content query. Invalid tags are rejected before writing. Updating only body retains title/id and makes its new words searchable.
concept: Language-aware search is not substring matching. English stemming relates run and running, and stop words may disappear. plainto_tsquery treats input as plain terms rather than exposing operator syntax. Binding the parameter separates query structure from user values. Choosing only title/body makes the searched domain explicit. The current small app computes its vector in the query; it does not yet add a GIN index or relevance ranking. Debouncing reduces calls but does not stop an old slow response arriving last. A request version guards publication of results, errors and loading state. That version coordinates the UI and is not a database record version. Explicitly JSON-encoding tags avoids the driver interpreting a JavaScript array as a PostgreSQL array.
flow: Construct a content vector and bound query
Publish only the newest request version
Show searching or the matching count
exercises: Rank by relevance with stable ties.
answers: Generate or backfill the same configured vector, verify behavior equivalence and then measure a larger fixture.
Reuse the tsquery for rank and filtering; break ties by a documented stable field.
Delay the first stub response, return the second and prove the second remains visible after both finish.
Decide whether language belongs to each note or the workspace, migrate deliberately and test language-specific stemming.
setup: Install dependencies in server and client separately. Follow the root README and .env.example for your development database. Run API scripts from server and frontend scripts from client. Tests require ASTRA_TEST_DATABASE_URL pointing at a dedicated astra_test_* database; they create an isolated schema rather than use development records.

title: Bookmark Manager: validated links and metadata
focus: runtime schemas, outbound policy and controlled network tests
model: Bookmarks store title, URL, collection, status and JSON tags. Saving a URL never fetches it. Explicit metadata preview proposes a title and URL without saving a bookmark.
before: The scaffold copied fields without substantive runtime validation and lacked a metadata boundary. Emitted ESM paths also needed correction for a normal Node start.
after: Zod validates create and partial updates. Metadata accepts configured exact HTTPS hosts on port 443, validates public IPv4 DNS answers, pins the connection, rejects redirects, and bounds headers/body/time. The UI applies a proposed title only if its URL still matches the request.
example: A controlled host returns title A & B, yielding A & B. A redirect to loopback is rejected without contacting its target. Private DNS, unlisted hosts, oversized bodies and timeouts fail. DNS finishing after timeout cannot start a transfer. A javascript: URL is rejected before insertion.
concept: Saving URL text and fetching it are distinct permission boundaries. The empty-by-default BOOKMARK_METADATA_HOSTS allowlist prevents ambient requests during ordinary saves. An allowed name can still resolve to a private address: validate its DNS answers, then pin a checked address into the real connection lookup while retaining the hostname for TLS verification. Otherwise a second DNS decision could differ from the checked result. Rejecting every redirect avoids a new unchecked target. One deadline covers DNS and response work, and delayed DNS checks the abort state before starting transport. The conservative policy supports only public IPv4 HTTPS and uncompressed HTML; it is not a universal website scraper. Tests substitute the connection factory to reach a local stub while retaining real response-status, size and timeout handling. No external website was contacted for verification.
flow: Validate the URL and configured host
Pin one public address for bounded transfer
Parse only a successful bounded response
Apply the title only if the form URL is unchanged
exercises: Explain disabled metadata capability before requesting.
Test mixed DNS answers and forbidden ports.
answers: Expose a capability flag without secrets and retain manual entry in every state.
Use a parser that neither executes scripts nor fetches resources; bound input first and render output as text.
Return public and private answers together and assert no transfer. Test non-443 ports and credentials separately.
Limit hops, revalidate and pin every target, retain one deadline/byte budget and forward no credentials. Keep redirects rejected until those cases are verified.
setup: Install dependencies in server and client separately. Follow the root README and .env.example for your development database. Run API scripts from server and frontend scripts from client. Tests require ASTRA_TEST_DATABASE_URL pointing at a dedicated astra_test_* database; they create an isolated schema rather than use development records. Metadata is disabled until BOOKMARK_METADATA_HOSTS contains exact HTTPS hostnames. Manual bookmark creation needs no metadata configuration. Verification used only a controlled local stub.
